title: A clear cola, a Super Bowl and a one-quarter boost
lede: Crystal Pepsi did not fail quietly. It tested well, launched loudly and won awards. Then people who had tried it once did not buy it again, and the company that made it said so in its annual report.

chapters.title: Three thousand formulas for a slow market
chapters.cap: taste variations Pepsi said it made over about 15 months before choosing one
chapters.body:
By 1991 soft drinks were a $47 billion retail business in the United States, and PepsiCo told shareholders that “growth had begun to slow down.” Consumers wanted variety, and a category of drinks without preservatives, known as “new age” beverages, was emerging.[^1] The Los Angeles Times reported that industry sales had grown 4% to 6% a year in the 1980s and were “generally flat in 1991.”[^6]

Pepsi’s answer was a cola with no caramel color. The company said it worked on it for about 15 months, created nearly 3,000 variations and tested with more than 5,000 consumers.[^5] It rejected dozens of names, among them Pepsi Clear and Pepsi Ice.[^6] The result had no caffeine and 130 calories per 12-ounce can against 150 for regular Pepsi.[^5]

pull.text: It’s not just Pepsi without the color.
pull.who: David Novak, Pepsi-Cola marketing executive, Associated Press, Apr 13, 1992[^5]

chapters.artCaption: The test-market package included a silver 12-ounce can and clear bottles with a blue and red label.[^5] Original illustration.

chapters.title: “Blowing off the shelves”
chapters.cap: promotional price of a two-liter bottle at one Rhode Island chain, with coupons, against a usual $1.49
chapters.body:
The test began in April 1992 in Providence, Dallas and across Colorado.[^5] Pepsi supported it with advertising and with price promotions. Over Memorial Day weekend one grocery chain in Providence sold two-liter bottles for 39 cents with coupons instead of the usual $1.49. “It’s blowing off the shelves,” a clerk in Cranston told the Los Angeles Times.[^6]

The same article carried the warning. The manager of an Albertson’s in Dallas said the drink was selling well and would not last: “People are trained to drink a brown cola, and that’s what they’ll eventually want.”[^6] Pepsi test-marketed for about six months, added a diet version, and in December announced national distribution.[^2][^9]

chapters.title: A Super Bowl, an inauguration and a $1 billion projection
chapters.cap: estimated advertising support for the national launch
chapters.body:
Crystal Pepsi was introduced nationally in the second week of December 1992.[^8] The following week Coca-Cola unveiled Tab Clear, and Pepsi answered with a number: Crystal Pepsi would take more than 2% of the $47 billion US soft drink market in its first year of national distribution, about $1 billion in retail sales.[^8] The New York Times put the advertising support at an estimated $40 million, starting with the Super Bowl on January 31.[^8]

The campaign opened on the eve of President Clinton’s inauguration[^14] and ran in the Super Bowl to Van Halen’s “Right Now” under the line “You’ve never seen a taste like this.”[^12][^22] In San Francisco, Pepsi paid nearly $3,000 a month per bus to wrap six buses end to end.[^13] In December a consumer research firm had named it the best new grocery product of 1992.[^10]

chapters.title: From hot product to punchline
chapters.cap: the period PepsiCo said the brand “particularly aided”
chapters.body:
In March 1993 the publisher of Beverage Digest said Crystal Pepsi had earned a full share point, and that a point was worth $474 million at retail.[^15] The same month the Associated Press reported that clear dish soap, clear mouthwash, clear deodorant and a clear beer were all arriving at once, under the headline that the trend looked like a short-term fad.[^14]

On October 2, 1993, Saturday Night Live ran a commercial parody for a clear gravy.[^31] PepsiCo’s annual report for the year was plain about it: the Crystal Pepsi products “particularly aided first quarter results, but did not significantly impact full year profits.” Because of “softening trends,” the product was “being refined” and would be “reintroduced in 1994 in a nondiet version only.”[^2]

chapters.title: The Pepsi name comes off the label
chapters.cap: the year the original was withdrawn and replaced by a citrus cola called Crystal
chapters.body:
In March 1994 The New York Times described the clear colas as “Pepsi’s most recent gimmick,” one that “has been deemed a dud and is undergoing an overhaul.”[^18] By July the replacement was reaching stores nationwide: a version with “a citrus cola taste,” aimed at teenagers. The word Pepsi was gone from the name. The label said “From the makers of Pepsi.”[^19]

Advertising Age opened its report with the sentence “The future of Crystal is anything but clear.” There was a single test commercial in four markets and no summer advertising plan.[^19] PepsiCo’s next annual report listed “significant declines in the Crystal Pepsi brands” in a year when its domestic case sales grew 6%.[^3][^4] We found no announcement of when the citrus version was dropped.
chapters.artCaption: By late 1993 the clear trend was a television joke: a gravy you could see through.[^31] Original illustration.

chapters.title: A flop becomes a collectible
chapters.cap: six-packs given away in the December 2015 sweepstakes
chapters.body:
In 2013 a competitive eater named Kevin Strahle posted a video of himself drinking a 20-year-old bottle. By June 2015 it had more than 11 million views and he was leading a campaign with a petition of more than 33,700 signatures and 15 billboards around Los Angeles.[^23] PepsiCo wrote back, and in December gave away 13,000 six-packs through its loyalty app.[^24][^25]

Retail runs followed in the summers of 2016 and 2017, in 20-ounce bottles at $1.79. PepsiCo’s 2017 release called it the “last return.”[^29][^32] It was not. In January 2022 the company marked the thirtieth anniversary with a contest for 300 winners.[^34]
